vignette:
Amir is a thirty-four-year-old married man who works as a publisher, a job that once felt stable and predictable. Nine months ago, his younger brother was stabbed during a mugging outside a downtown subway station. Amir did not witness the attack itself, but he arrived at the hospital minutes afterward, walking into the emergency bay as his brother lay on a gurney, blood soaking through a torn jacket, a nurse pressing gauze to his neck. What Amir remembers most vividly is not his brother’s face but the sound of the monitor beeping irregularly and the sight of a discarded pair of surgical scissors glinting on a tray near the curtain. Those moments come back to him in disconnected pieces—the beeping, the scissors, the smell of antiseptic—that he cannot arrange into a single coherent story. Sometimes, when he is trying to fall asleep, he hears the monitor again, a high-pitched tone that makes his chest tighten, and the memory replays like a short film he cannot stop.

Since that night, Amir has become acutely aware of danger in his surroundings. He studies the faces of strangers on the bus, scanning for the particular set of features he associates with the man who was arrested—a certain hardness around the jaw, a flatness in the eyes. He notices potential weapons everywhere: a letter opener on a colleague’s desk, a pair of kitchen shears in his own drawer, the metal edge of a chair. This constant vigilance has made him avoid unfamiliar places entirely; he drives the same route to work every day and will not take the bus, even when his car is in the shop. The fatigue from this unrelenting watchfulness leaves him drained by midafternoon, and when he is very tired, his mind drifts more easily back to the hospital room. A wave of exhaustion will suddenly trigger a flash of the gurney, and then he is scanning the room again, looking for something sharp, something wrong.

Being vulnerable—undressed in the shower, or lying in bed next to his wife—makes him feel exposed in a way he cannot explain. When he is naked, he finds himself checking the bedroom door, listening for footsteps, as if the threat is already inside the house. This hypervigilance feeds the memories: the more he watches for danger, the more the fragmented images surface. And each time the memory plays, he becomes more certain that he missed something that night, that he should have arrived earlier, that he should have seen it coming. That belief drives him to scan even harder, creating a loop that tightens with each turn. His wife has noticed that he no longer sits with his back to the door in restaurants, and that he has stopped going to the grocery store after dark. At work, he has declined two meetings in unfamiliar parts of the city, offering vague excuses about scheduling conflicts.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was a moment on a quiet Tuesday afternoon. He was sitting at his desk, reviewing a manuscript, when he heard a janitor drop a metal bucket in the hallway. The clatter sent him out of his chair, heart pounding, and he stood frozen for several seconds before realizing what had happened. He is afraid of what this is doing to his marriage, and he is hoping that talking about it will make the film stop playing. But what frightens him most is the thought that if he stops watching for danger, something terrible will happen to someone he loves again.
